prime.problem: A language model answers by running once per output token, and requests need very different numbers of runs. If the server hands the GPU a fixed batch and waits for all of it, finished requests keep occupying slots and new ones can't start, so most of each expensive weight read is wasted.
prime.fits: First paper card. Course 2's step formula showed that one decode step reads every weight once, so a full batch is nearly free. This card is the scheduling idea that keeps the batch full, plus the batching trick that makes such a mixed batch runnable.
expect: the three shape cases that block batching (C2)
selective batching: flatten to [ΣL, H], split only for attention
prime.goal: Explain why re-choosing the batch every iteration needs selective batching to work, and estimate the waste of request-level batching from a set of output lengths.

attend: In Fig 3, which two separate costs does request-level batching impose on x2 and on the late joiner x3?
Why does iteration-level scheduling immediately create the problem of batching requests at different points in their life?
Which operations in a layer care which request a token belongs to, and why is attention the only one?
Why does leaving attention unbatched cost almost nothing, according to Orca's own argument about weight reads?
Why is the simulated gain about 2× when outputs are uniform on 1–1,024, and what would change it?

must: The serving system hears back only when a whole batch ends → finished requests keep being computed and new ones wait → about half of all slot-iterations are wasted when a batch lives as long as its longest request (49% in our sim) → iteration-level scheduling returns and admits requests after every iteration

Re-picking the batch each iteration mixes prefills and decodes at different token indices → their tensors have different shapes → naive batching needs same phase and same length, which gets exponentially rarer as B grows → selective batching flattens all tokens to [ΣL, H] for every weight op and splits only for attention

Weight ops reuse one weight read across all tokens → batching them is the whole point; attention has no weights and each request reads its own KV → running it per request loses no reuse → splitting just before attention costs almost nothing
elevated: Modern engines keep Orca's flat token batch but run one ragged attention kernel over all requests via a block table → same idea, but launch overhead and occupancy improve (FlashInfer's ragged tensors)
reference: the Fig 2 two-layer stack names (Triton, FasterTransformer)
the simulator's parameters (3,000 requests, Poisson, B_MAX = 64, seed 0)
the exact TTFT table values at 5 and 8 req/s

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, write three sentences: what goes wrong with request-level batching, what iteration-level scheduling changes, and why that change forces selective batching. Then draw the Fig 5 layer as boxes and mark which ones are batched.
checklist: a batch runs until its longest request ends, so early finishers waste slots and late arrivals queue
the scheduler picks the batch before every iteration, so requests leave and join one token at a time
the mixed batch has different shapes (phase, length, token index)
flatten all tokens for Linear, LayerNorm, GeLU, Add; split per request only for attention
attention has no weights to share, so running it per request costs nothing in reuse

retrieve.q: Explain why iteration-level scheduling alone, without selective batching, would leave an H100 stuck at tiny batches.
answer: requests picked at different points in their life have different phases, lengths or token indices
tensor batching needs identical shapes, which becomes exponentially less likely as B grows
so only a few matching requests could run together, the regime where the H100 makes about 205 tok/s

retrieve.q: Trace the Fig 5 iteration: x1 and x2 decoding, x3 and x4 prefilling 2 and 3 tokens. What shape enters QKV Linear, what happens at Split, and where do x1's earlier keys and values come from?
answer: 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7 tokens, so [7, H] in and [7, 3H] out
Split gives each request its own slice; each runs attention separately
x1 and x2 fetch cached K/V from the Attention K/V manager; x3 and x4 have none yet
Merge rebuilds [7, H] for Attn Out Linear and the MLP

retrieve.q: When would you still choose static request-level batching today, and what does iteration-level scheduling not decide for you?
answer: offline jobs whose requests all have the same known length: no waste, simpler
it doesn't decide which requests fit in KV memory; that's the scheduler and paging
packing whole prompts into a decode iteration makes that iteration long (the generation stall)

compare.q: Orca's hybrid iteration and vLLM's prefill-only iteration both admit new prompts eagerly. What does Orca's design get right that makes its iterations mixed, and what problem does that same design create for running users?
answer: selective batching lets prompt tokens and decode tokens share one weight read
but a whole prompt in the iteration makes it compute-bound and long
every decoding user waits for it: 74.04 ms instead of 7.36 in the running example
Sarathi fixes it by bounding the prompt tokens per iteration

compare.q: Course 2's engine-design sim showed static batching's TTFT collapsing (7,314 ms → 46 ms interleaved). What in this card explains the collapse mechanistically, and what did the course-2 sim abstract away?
answer: static batching makes new requests wait for the whole running batch to drain
iteration-level scheduling bounds that wait at one iteration
the course-2 sim assumed mixed batches just work; Orca shows they need selective batching to be runnable

predict.q: Real chat outputs are long-tailed: most answers are short, a few run to thousands of tokens. Compared with the card's uniform 1–1,024 outputs, does request-level batching waste more or less, and does the 1.93× gap grow or shrink? Commit first.
predict.answer: More waste, bigger gap. A static batch lives as long as its longest member, and a long tail makes the longest member much longer than the mean, so a larger share of slot-iterations computes finished requests. The card says as much: longer-tailed real traffic wastes more. With Orca's own short outputs (up to 128) the waste and the gap would be smaller.

apply.task: By hand: a static batch of four requests needs 3, 10, 5 and 2 output tokens. (a) How many iterations does the batch run, how many slot-iterations exist, and what share is wasted? (b) Under iteration-level scheduling, at which iteration does each slot free up? (c) Now three requests decoding and two new prompts of 5 and 4 tokens share one iteration: what is ΣL, and what is the QKV output shape for Llama-3.1-8B (32 query heads + 2 × 8 KV heads, head dim 128)?
apply.done: You wrote the waste as a fraction, the four free-up iterations, and the [ΣL, width] shape, before checking.
apply.hint: Check after trying: (a) 10 iterations × 4 slots = 40 slot-iterations; 3 + 10 + 5 + 2 = 20 are used, so 50% are wasted. (b) The slots free after iterations 2, 3, 5 and 10, and a waiting request can take each one at the next iteration. (c) 3 + 5 + 4 = 12 tokens, so the QKV output is [12, 6,144].
